the human auditory cortex exhibits tonotopy, that this tonotopy is organized in a complex manner, and that it is related to sound categories.
the human auditory cortex exhibits a complex organization of tonotopy and spectral tuning and that this organization extends to voice and speech selective regions.

the human auditory cortex contains a tonotopically organized map of spectral tuning width, and that this map extends into higher-order and category selective regions, where the low-frequency portions are biased toward the spectral characteristics of speech/voice.

the processing of natural sounds in human auditory cortex, and the neural transformations underlying this processing.
the processing of natural sounds in the human auditory system.
the neural representation of complex sounds and their relation to the tonotopic organization of the human auditory cortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the processing of complex natural sounds is a highly organized and complex process that involves multiple cortical regions with different tuning characteristics, which are all part of a larger network that enables the transformation of the incoming sensory information to higher level representations of sound.
the auditory cortex of the human brain is a complex system that can be described by the interaction of a tonotopic map and the processing of natural sounds.

the processing of natural sounds in human auditory cortex is not a simple transformation of tonotopy, as has been previously assumed, but rather a combination of multiple mechanisms that include the transformation of tonotopic information into spectral representations, and the transformation of these representations into sound category-specific information.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human auditory cortex is organized in a tonotopic fashion with a high degree of spectral tuning.

natural sounds are represented in the human auditory brain in a tonotopic fashion, and that this tonotopic representation is biased by the spectral content of the sounds, with a bias toward the spectral characteristics of human speech and voice.

the auditory cortex contains two types of frequency maps, one that represents the physical frequency spectrum of the incoming sound, and a second map that represents the spectral content of the sound that is relevant to the sound's meaning or category.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tonotopic and category-selective representations of natural sounds coexist in the human auditory system and that the latter can be understood as a transformation of the former.

spectral preference and tuning in the human auditory system are not confined to the primary auditory areas, but extend to higher order and even voice-selective auditory regions, suggesting that these regions also operate at a sensory (spectral) level.
tonotopic and tuning maps are not confined to the primary auditory cortex but extend to the entire auditory system.
